utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. Case Number IT-00-39-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Crncalo, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound which the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Yes. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to continue the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We notice there's a discrepancy on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you use your microphone, we could hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry, Your Honour. Your Honour, good morning. My apologies. I was just grabbing hold of some headphones. We notice there's a discrepancy on the transcript against the time 9.03, it says upon commencing at 9.01, so something's mechanically gone wrong there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be both 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's another issue. I was thinking to the mechanical question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just took the opportunity to draw your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No further observations, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, immediately before the adjournment yesterday, I had put it to you that when you were arrested as you had described in your evidence, that in fact your rifle, your hunting rifle, was not leaning against the door of your house but that you were, in fact, in the street carrying your rifle. Thinking back to those events, is it not correct that you were actually holding your rifle at the time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My rifle was leaning against the wall of the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be something wrong with the sound Mr. Crncalo receives. Is it now better, Mr. Crncalo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever there's any problem, please tell me. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do I understand Mr. Crncalo didn't get --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, you didn't get my full question? Because you seem to have got it and answered it. You got my full question and answered: "My rifle was leaning against the wall of the house." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not against the door, against the wall of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. You said in your statement at paragraph 24 -- sorry, 26, you say that, "Ten days after my arrest, Serbs started a campaign to have all non-Serbs leave the local Pale Municipality." And you say: "This was accomplished by designated Serbs coming to my community and telling us that it was better for us to leave now in peace rather than staying and suffering trouble later." The translation that you will now be hearing is back into translation into your own language. "Accomplished by designated Serbs," what do you mean by that? Designated in what sense?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I see it, they were activists belonging to some party, probably the SDS. And they were sent to exert propaganda and force us or prevail upon us to leave our houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say "probably" -- you say, "belonging to some party, probably the SDS," that suggests that you don't actually know, that that's your own speculation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There still seems to be problems with the sound. The problem is, Mr. Crncalo, that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No Interpretation] When I'm speaking, I can hear my own voice echoing back at me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, I do understand that you do not receive full translation. Is that correct? [German spoken]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear the interpretation fully, but I have an echo, and I can hear my own voice when I'm speaking. It echoes back at me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not a translation matter, but it's a rather technical matter. Could we ask the assistance of the technicians to see that we can get rid of this echo. We wait for the arrival of a technician to... May I ask if the technician thinks that the matter has been solved -- no, he's -- somebody's arriving. It's a matter of echo if the witness himself speaks, so perhaps you could... Mr. Crncalo, could you please now speak a few words and see whether the echo is gone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can check. Yes, I think it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see you're nodding and everything's fine. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, just going back to immediately before your arrest, there was a well-publicised incident in Sarajevo, wasn't there, on the 1st of March 1992 when members of a Muslim organisation known as the Green Berets attacked a wedding party, and the Serb groom was killed? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that from the media, that that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that contributed or caused a significant rise of tension, didn't it, in Pale, disregarding anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The matter was discussed and talked about, and as far as tensions are concerned, tensions among the people, both ethnic groups living in Pale, they didn't happen with respect to that event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that event didn't contribute to any rise of tension in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to feel that, that that was it. Probably I would have noticed had it been the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that after that event, and I'm talking now about the period shortly after, in March or April 1992, the same organisation, the Green Berets, stopped buses coming into -- going into Sarajevo from Pale and would take money and documents from Serb passengers and physically harass them? Do you recall anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't leave Pale either to go to Sarajevo, and I can't answer that. I can't really say how it is exactly. I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think what I asked you was whether you recall that. Are you saying that at the time you didn't know anything about such matters?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were checkpoints towards Sarajevo and towards Pale. But I myself didn't see what those people at the checkpoint in Sarajevo did. I didn't go there, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that they were what might be rather crudely refer to as "Muslim checkpoints"?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall that on the 4th of April, the village of Lapisnica, which is a mainly Serb -- was a mainly Serb village was attacked by the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but I do know where Lapisnica is, I know that very well, and I know who lives there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is it from the centre of Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's closer to Sarajevo than it is to Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that lead -- that incident, did that lead to the SJB, the public security service, setting up barricades?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which public security service are you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, public security station. Mr. Crncalo, that's what I'm talking about. So the answer to the question -- well, my question was: "Did that incident lead to the public security station setting up barricades"?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public security service at the Pale Municipality, is that what you're referring to, or are you referring to some other municipality?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Pale Municipality.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was -- or rather, Lapisnica is a village closer to Sarajevo than it is to Pale, so I really don't know the arrival of the checkpoint, the barricade. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me be the one to put the questions to you, then. Do you know of any public security station, from wherever, setting up barricades after that incident between Pale and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the checkpoints at Pale, but I wasn't able to move around there. As for some barricades, such as was shown on television when Sarajevo was cut across with barricades, I don't know that anything like that happened or was set up in the Pale Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when do you say checkpoints -- you say you know about checkpoints at Pale. When do you say that checkpoints were first set up in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, give as good a date as you can give, then please, Mr. Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of April, these, or rather the checkpoints started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they start?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that in front of a tunnel called Stambolcici tunnel that that's where I saw it. Then I saw them near the Famos company. Then I saw another one a little before you get to the railway station at a junction, somewhere there. I know about those checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who set up these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were set up by the army, the soldiers that were in Pale at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "the army," you mean the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have the insignia of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which army do you mean? You said "the army."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say "the army." The Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska didn't exist at that time, Mr. Crncalo, did it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know it didn't exist, but you could see that they were -- that those soldiers belonged to - or let me put it this way - to the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how could you see that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could see that on the basis of a statement made by Mr. Karadzic when he encouraged his people and said that the army was with the Serbs and that they shouldn't be afraid of anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which army did you understand Mr. Karadzic was referring to, then? That would have been the JNA, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, on the 4th of June 1992, there was an attack by Muslims on a convoy of soldiers in the -- in Zepa near to Pale, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Zepa isn't really near Pale. Zepa is near Sokolac and Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. How far from Pale is Zepa?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went into Zepa. Probably about 50 kilometres, about 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about 45 or about 45 soldiers were killed by Muslims in that attack, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number. I don't know how many people were killed, those young men who were Serbs from Pale. But I do know that the number was quite high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you're quite right. They were Serbs from Pale. And do you know that an agreement -- say if you don't know anything about this, but do you know that an agreement had been reached with the Muslims for safe passage of that convoy, and that agreement was violated?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that agreement. But I do know that there was fighting at Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those killed were entirely or very largely from Pale, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. And if you like, I can comment on that. The statement of a mother and the behaviour of a woman when her husband was killed at Zepa and the mother whose son was killed at Zepa, I can tell you about that if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Crncalo, we can all sympathise and understand, and I think imagine what statements would be made by grieving mothers and wives. And while recognising it, I think we can move on to specific questions. Mr. Crncalo, that incident gave rise to an enormous increase in tension as between Serbs and Muslims in Pale, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And times were most difficult then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And another reason times were most difficult was that there had by that time been a very large wave of Serb refugees arriving in Pale from Sarajevo, hadn't there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when I say "large," something of the order of 30.000. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a population from outside -- they were all coming in, a big flow coming in. Now, the exact number, I really can't say. I didn't -- I wasn't able to learn about that, nor was I able to see it. I couldn't see all the people coming into Pale, where they were put up, how they were accommodated, until we left -- well, I don't know. But you could see that there were a lot of people, too many people in Pale, coming in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, I certainly don't want to unrealistically press you to any sort of head count. That simply wouldn't be fair or realistic. What I'm inviting you, therefore, to do is to confirm that a figure of 30.000, that's a very large number, but that's consistent with what you were able to observe at that time in Pale, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the inflow of populace was great.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, I'm going to invite you, please, to try not to be tempted to refer back to what you've already said and look at the particular question I'm asking. Is a figure of 30.000 consistent with what you were able to observe at that time in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm under oath here to tell the truth, and I'm telling you the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the answer --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not my question, Mr. Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, what Mr. Stewart would like to know from you is the following. He said 30.000. You said a big flow. And he would like to know whether what you call a big flow could be approximately 30.000, or that you would say no, it was far less or far more. He just wants to compare what you understand by a big flow and whether that would be contradicted by the 30.000 or that you say, well, it could have been 30.000. That's the only thing he would like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked yesterday how many inhabitants the Municipality of Pale had, and I said about 15.000. Now I'm thinking about this. Did the population double after the arrival of these new people? I'm wondering. And I'm turning the film back in my mind to the image of that municipality, what it looked like at the time. Well, I don't think that it was 30.000 because 30.000 is a lot, a great deal, a great deal of people. But the frequency of people coming in was great. Now, 30.000 seems to me, I'm trying to see how many people 15.000 is, and then when you ask me about 30.000, I don't think I can agree to a figure of 30.000. It seems too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm satisfied, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you at this very moment. Are we listening to background information, are we listening to questions and answers about credibility of the witness, or are we listening to evidence relating to justification of responses if such things happened as you put it to Mr. Crncalo? It's a bit unclear for the Chamber, and as I said yesterday it's also a bit unclear whether so much time spent on whether a big flow could be 30.000 or perhaps 20.000 or 40.000 is of that relevance for what is this case about. And I also wondered to what extent, and I'm addressing you, Mr. Hannis, at this moment, and I apologise for -- Mr. Hannis, what's the position of the Prosecution in relation to, first of all, incidents -- well, let's say initiated or caused by Muslim armed forces; that's one. Whether that took place. And the second one, what that would mean for your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's in the nature of tu quoque as being a justification for the actions that the Serb take, yes, we would object to that. But I understood that perhaps Mr. Stewart was asking those kind of questions of this witness just to try to establish what Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond level of awareness he had about events in general and happening in his area, and therefore going to his credibility. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's not entirely clear to me whether it's a credibility issue or whether it's a background issue. Mr. Stewart, could you give a clue to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, really -- I suggest that sometimes it would be, with respect, we would proceed much better if the Trial Chamber could simply wait to see where these questions lead, and then it would quickly become apparent. So far as the numbers are concerned, I entirely accept what Your Honour has said. It doesn't really matter for these purposes whether it's 20.000, 30.000, or 40.000. But it's a reasonable starting question to ask the witness whether he agrees that it's consistent with the figure which I have been given on my instructions as to the figure. And I was then immediately going on in the light of the exchange, and it's not that easy to get a straight answer on that from the witness, was simply going on to say, all right, Mr. Crncalo, can we agree it was many, many thousands, and that is enough. But actually to answer Your Honour's question as will become apparent, this is important lead-in information to an important point which is exactly what cross-examination and any examination of a witness should involve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps -- let me say the following. You say these are important points; fine, the Chamber accepts that. The quicker you are to come to important points, the -- let me say, the quicker you come to the importance of the point, the better it is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think the transcript will show, Your Honour, that the Defence has proceeded as quickly as could reasonable be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's stop the discussions. I hope you got the message. I also understand that you do not fully agree. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll leave others to judge in the end, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, can we, as I think you probably heard that, we can agree many, many thousands of refugees came into Pale from Sarajevo, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that. As to the number that you mentioned, that's a very large figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're not going over that ground again, Mr. Crncalo. The numbers and the heightened tensions and the incident which happened in Zepa led, among other things, to a very high feeling of insecurity among the Muslim population in Pale, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Muslim population were so concerned about their position in the light of the influx of refugees from Sarajevo and the increase in tensions that they, through their representatives, made a request that arrangements should be made to enable Muslims to leave Pale, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If anyone should be aware of such requests, I should be aware of it. I don't think there was ever any such request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you know nothing, do you, about a request on the basis of which on the 18th of June 1992 the Municipal Assembly of Pale issued a direction relating to change of residence of Muslims and Croat nationals? So you know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you think that that was some sort of a solution, I'm not aware of that because I went to the president of the municipality on a number of occasions and asked for the possibility of staying in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, the question was whether you knew about a request on the basis of which the municipal assembly issued a direction relating to a change. So what Mr. Stewart puts to you is that there was a decision taken on the 18th of June as a consequence of a request. Are you aware of such a request, whether you made that request or anyone else made that request? Are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Cmeric suggests that the answer which appears in the English version of the transcript as, "If you think that was some sort of a solution," that, in fact, the witness said something which should be translated: "If you think that was some sort of municipal decision." There seems to be quite a discrepancy there. I don't know the answer because I simply raise the question as suggested to me by Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, we might have a translation problem at this moment. When you said: "If you think that that was some sort of..." And then it's unclear what you then said. And you then continued: "I'm not aware of that because I went to the president," et cetera. What did you say when you said, "If you think that was some sort of ..."? Could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat that. I was never in a position to know what the municipal organs wanted or to know what their intentions were. With certain people, I went to ask the municipality to remain in the Municipality of Pale. As to the decisions they adopted on their own as to what they would do with us, the Muslims, I knew nothing about this. It was only when we had to sit and get into the buses and go to Sarajevo that things were clear to me. It was clear that we had to change our place of residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand your answer to be that you do not know about the decision, and you do not know about a request related to that decision. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I simply then comment -- I hope Your Honour will see the importance of the point we were leading up to. But so far as this witness is concerned, in light of his saying that he knows nothing about this, I don't need any -- that in fact shouldn't -- it's not my obligation to put any more to this witness in relation to that matter because he said he doesn't know, so I leave that topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Except to this extent, Mr. Crncalo, that the detailed arrangements that were then made and posted in a way that you described yesterday with a notice being pinned up in Pale, were arrangements for buses to go on particular days from particular places, and those were practical arrangements to implement the understood procedure that a significant number of Muslims were going to leave Pale? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question isn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. It became a rather long question, Mr. Crncalo. I apologise for that. You described yesterday how a notice was put up, a written notice concerning Muslims leaving Pale. You remember that. What I'm saying to you is that as in response to a request made in some form or another by Muslim representatives and an agreement between Serbs and Muslims, that Muslims could and in many cases wanted to leave Pale, what was posted up included that such and such a bus would be going on such and such a day from such and such a place, that such and such another bus would be going on such and such day from such and such a place. That was included in that written notice, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whatever the background, and we've heard a lot about the background, it was a fact, wasn't it, that at that time a significant number of Muslims did want to leave Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I asked it, Mr. Crncalo. So please do.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A minute ago, you put an ambiguous question to me. And my answer was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I apologise for any ambiguity, Mr. Crncalo. If you want clarification of any question at any time, please don't hesitate to say so. But please do take the opportunity of clarifying any answer.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered the previous question incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, just make it clear which question and which answer you would wish to correct, Mr. Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned an agreement between the Muslims and the Serbs for the Muslims to leave Pale voluntarily, and you also mentioned buses. And when I said yes, I was thinking of the buses when they arrived. There was no agreement. We were forced to leave Pale. Please, don't make me answer incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, the last question was, as a matter of fact, whether there were many Muslims who wanted to leave Pale at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think he's referring to the question before that, which began on page 15, near the end, and went on for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that he refers to that. But I'd like him to answer the last question after he made the correction. If you would answer the question put to you last by Mr. Stewart, and that was whatever the background was about the buses and whatever happened, is it true that at that time there was a considerable number of Muslims that wanted to leave Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. None of us wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, this I've put to you as perhaps clarifying the position: You had not wanted the situation which had arisen; nobody wanted that situation with the enormous influx of refugees from Sarajevo, the violence that had occurred. You had not wanted that situation. But given the situation that you had got at the end of June and the beginning of July, it was a fact, wasn't it, that at that point a large number of Muslims wanted to leave Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to repeat this a number of times. None of us wanted to leave our homes, our property and to go out into the world like a beggar. But we had to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A large number of Muslims preferred to leave Pale at the beginning of July 1992 to staying there, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't want to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, Mr. Crncalo. A large number of Serbs, given the situation they were in at the end of June, beginning of July, of the two choices to stay in Pale and leave Pale, a large number of Muslims -- sorry, did I have a slip of the tongue? A large number of Muslims preferred the choice of leaving Pale, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one wanted to leave their homes on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I've put it enough times, and the Trial Chamber can see clearly where we've got to, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's quite clear. I was already asking myself whether the question was not already answered three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It wasn't answered, Your Honour, but the position is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The position is quite clear, Mr. Stewart. And one of the problems, of course, is if you say "under those circumstances," it very much depends on what is included in those circumstances. If you would include -- let's just assume that there were threats that bad things would happen if they would stay, then of course there comes a certain point when you move your feet towards the buses. And if you say that is included in those circumstances, then of course the preference would be to go to the bus and not stay. But that's of courses the imprecision and that's of course the whole problem of these kind of questions, that it does not always clarify the issue. So perhaps it better to have waited with these comments until after the questions had been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I say, Your Honour, I can't see how counsel can do anything else when referring to the circumstances. The witness was in Pale, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not further discuss it at this moment in the presence of the witness. I gave a few comments. If there's any need to further discuss that, we could do that at a later stage. And then I might be clearer in my explanation. But let's now move on to the next subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened, Mr. Crncalo, was that the municipal authorities did give support and cooperation to enable a large number of Muslims to leave Pale safely, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they did, those Muslims, they did leave Pale safely, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken out. We didn't go away voluntarily. We were escorted by the police and the army to the demarcation line of the conflict area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was, I put it to you, that they did leave Pale safely, didn't they? And can you confirm that the answer to that question is yes, they did leave Pale safely?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have answered your question, and I said that we went under escort of men from the Municipality of Pale. We went as far as the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the Muslims leaving Pale come to any physical harm by the time they reached the demarcation line?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. This is what I can say: I think that we went there without suffering any injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to ask you a couple of relatively short points, Mr. Crncalo, in your statement at paragraph 28, you refer to the visit of Mr. Nikola Koljevic, and you say "after approximately 10 minutes, Nikola Koljevic accompanied by two active police" - there's a bit of tautology there - "FNU Stanar and FNU Jovicic arrived." Can you confirm that Mr. Stana and Mr. Jovicic, they were not part of Mr. Koljevic's personal entourage, were they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were security for him, and they were active policemen in the Pale police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had his own security, didn't he? Quite separately from those men, Mr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you were there, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another point, you say in your statement, paragraph 44, you learned that the three mosques in the Pale area were destroyed. There were, in fact, only two mosques in Pale, weren't there? One at Podvitez and one at, I think it's Praca. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one mosque in Praca, another in Podvitez, and a third in Bogovici. All three mosques were destroyed. The one in Podvitez, a village near Pale, there was a cemetery that was levelled to the ground there. And there are no signs indicating that people were once buried there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was going to look at the transcript to remind myself of the name of that other village, but it doesn't appear at the moment on the transcript. But -- what's it called?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Crncalo. How far is that from the centre of Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 45 of your statement, you refer to a number of Muslim families you say who refused to leave the Pale area July 1992 and were killed, and then you give a list of individuals. Do you have first-hand knowledge of any of those people being killed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of them or only some of them? And if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who didn't want to go with us from the Municipality of Pale, I've provided their names, and they have been recorded. They didn't want to leave, but they were all killed, not just some of them. But all of those who remained were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Would you please seek clarification whether the witness understands exactly first-hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was about to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally witness the killing of any of those people -- you might want to look at paragraph 45 or be given paragraph 45 of your statement. I think I must put the question to you again, Mr. Crncalo. It seemed to have gone too quickly to get picked up. Actually it was one of my simpler questions, Mr. Crncalo. Now, do you see paragraph 45? It's the last paragraph in your statement. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally witness the killing of any of the people whom you mention there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, you yourself should be able to see that I wasn't in a position to see this, to witness this. These people stayed on, and I left. So I couldn't see them, I couldn't personally witness them being killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what's the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the bodies were exhumed, I attended the burials. After they had been exhumed, I attended the burials. That's the source of my information. I can mention the names of the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Ziba Karic, for example, what do you specifically know about the death of Ziba Karic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the death of Ziba Karic, I don't know anything. But she is Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond not alive any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can agree about that, Mr. Crncalo; she's not alive any more. But she died of natural causes after the war, didn't she? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: She wasn't alive when the war ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she die of natural causes, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can provide you a direct answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: About her. I don't know exactly what she died of in her case. I don't know exactly how Ziba Karic died. As for the others, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's be just clear about that, then, Mr. Crncalo. Your evidence which is here in this statement that "I know that some Muslim families who refused to leave the Pale area in July 1992 were killed." Then goes on specifically to name individuals included in that category among whom Ziba Karic. So your statement is very clear. You are saying in your statement, in accordance with your solemn declaration you are telling this Trial Chamber that Ziba Karic was killed. But it is now clear, isn't it, that you simply do not know whether that is true or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the person called Ziba Karic, I don't know exactly what happened to her. She wasn't alive when the war ended. But I know about the other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you accept -- this is the last question I need to put to you on this, Mr. Crncalo. Do you accept that you must withdraw your evidence there in paragraph 45 in relation to Ziba Karic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't accept that. I can't withdraw what I said there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, in your statement you say Ziba Karic was killed. You just told us that you do not know how she died. Mr. Stewart is asking you whether you agree that your statement is, in respect of her, incorrect and should be withdrawn because you cannot confirm that she was killed; the only thing you know is that, at least it's what you told us, that she died. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say she died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If someone is not alive any more, then they die, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this, if I may be allowed to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first go to you said in your statement she was killed, which means that her death was caused by someone else. Now you tell us that you do not know how she died, which leaves it open that she died by natural causes. Therefore, Mr. Stewart seeks confirmation that your statement is incorrect in this respect since you do not know whether her death was caused by another person or whether she died for other -- by other causes. Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Is there any need for further questions to the witness, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just one or two questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. Re-examined by Mr. Hannis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, you were being asked by Mr. Stewart about when you left Pale. And I think the two of you were having a difficult time getting that question answered. You said you had two choices. But in spite of the fact that you did not want to leave Pale, you did get on the bus. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Stewart said you had two choices. Perhaps if I phrase those two choices to you in a different way, it might be easier to answer. Do you see your two choices as leaving Pale alive on the one hand or staying and being killed as your two choices?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we saw what the situation was and what could happen, we all decided to save our lives and to leave our property to its fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Witness, if I understood you correctly, you said that when you were about to leave Pale, you signed some papers to the effect that you were exchanging your property for a property in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Now, once you were in Sarajevo, were you able to take possession of that property?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not able to take possession because the premise, the house, was half destroyed by a shell that fell on it. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. But the papers were in order, were they not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. The papers were as they were. But I said yesterday that I signed them in the manner in which I had to sign them. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. Now, let's move on to another area and subject if we may. In your statement on several occasions, you make a distinction between what you call the Chetniks and the Serbs. If I understand you correctly, do you wish to say when you use the word "Chetnik" that you're referring to the members of the Radical Party alone?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just members of the Radical Party; not all Serbs are Chetniks. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. What you mentioned as being the Red Berets, are you able to tell us who they were under?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Malko Koroman said that he couldn't keep the Red Berets under his control for long. So that statement of mine, when I said that, that could mean that Malko Koroman could have been in charge of the Red Berets himself. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] When you said with respect to Mr. Koroman, and I'm quoting you [In English], "that is not able to afford the security of the Muslim community." [Interpretation] Did you gain the impression that this would make you leave or that the situation was beyond his power?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say exactly. I can't know what was happening in those structures exactly. My vision was as it was, and his statement that he wasn't able to guarantee our safety and security as free citizens was probably an incentive on his part to persuade us to leave our houses. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, Mr. Kovacevic, I think, was the president of the municipality, was he not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. At the beginning, it was Slobodan Kovacevic. Later on, he was replaced by Starcevic. I don't know his first name, but I do know Kovacevic. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But Mr. Kovacevic was a member of the SDS party, was he not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly he was. I don't know who was a member of the party, who all the members were. But as the SDS party was the main party in Pale, then I assume that's correct. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, when you say, and I'm quoting again [In English], "the president of the municipality did not believe that the Muslims were told to leave the city," [Interpretation] are you of the opinion that he was sincere in making that statement?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what the situation was like and what those political leaders in our municipality behaved like. Everybody wanted to leave a good impression on the population, the population that was suffering at the time in difficult circumstances. They could say what they wanted, but when they shifted us between one and the other for the same issues and both were in charge, I think that you can conclude yourself that they were just throwing the ball into the other person's court and shifting us from one to the other and that we had to go. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. But perhaps the language you use in saying "did not believe," that phrase, that is an observation of fact. It is the impression you gained, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think he was sincere in what he told us. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one relatively simple question for you. In the English version of your witness interview you gave to the high court in Sarajevo, there appears a certain type Crncalo, but I was asking myself whether it was Crncelo or Crncalo. Could you explain to us whether --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says on the screen now, that's my proper surname, the correct way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's your name --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: With an A, not an E. It's Crncalo with an A, not an E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But in your statement, and perhaps I read to you the part that I'm referring to, is that: "I was not alone with Radomir Kojic. There were other neighbours present. Rizat Smajic Ferhat Hrvo, Tajib Crncelo, it says." Is that a mistake? Should that be Crncalo as well or is there a person whose name is Tajib Crncelo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my brother, Tajib Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then my next question would be cousins of yours. There seemed perhaps to be some confusion. Are you aware of any family member ever arrested for trading weapons or selling weapons or buying weapons or illegal-weapon trade? So apart from the two names, are you aware of any such arrest, well, let's say in that period 1991-1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would probably have to have known -- have to know about that, but I don't know. The two men that I mentioned yesterday, I didn't go alone. I was with five other people to intervene with Malko Koroman to release them from the police station. It wasn't only those two. There were 19 other young -- there were 19 young men, including the two names I gave yesterday. But for the unlawful sale of anything, whether cigarettes or weapons, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at another moment, at another place?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The questions of the Bench, do they give any reason for the parties to raise any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No additional questions, but the point you raised about correcting the spelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have something to talk about, but we can talk about that when the witness leaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I looked at the original, whether it was an A or an E, I think thought it was an A, so therefore I thought it was incorrectly transcribed to the English. I wouldn't say translated, but transcribed. Mr. Crncalo, since you've answered all the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench, this concludes your evidence in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming and for answering the questions, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. Madam usher is trying to lead you to another door.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point I wanted to raise, the name Tajib Crncalo that you saw an E in one place instead of an A, his name appears a second time in the statement spelled correctly. On the following page, a few lines lower than it is on the preceding pages, right after the name Fadil Dzaferagic. And I noted also that I think there are two places where Malko Koroman's name is spelled Karaman, but I think it's clear from the context that we're talking about the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Hannis, I do understand that your next witness will arrive only tomorrow and therefore could be examined not any earlier than by next Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's also clear to the parties that we would sit next week only for two days. That's Monday and Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will it be one witness or ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We only have one witness scheduled. That's our last viva voce witness from Sanski Most Municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't believe that he will take two full days. I believe he will probably take more than one, but I don't believe he'll take two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can confer with Mr. Harmon to see if it were possible to condense him to one day if that were better for the Court, that one full day as opposed to one and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not specifically. And apart from that, if you say you do not see that his examination will take two full days, that would include cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe his entire examination will not take two full days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, there's -- of course, the sooner the witness could be excused, the better it is for him so he can return home. But there's no specific interest of the Chamber to have him finish by -- of course, if it can be done, it should be done. Then we have on our programme I think at least the reading in of 92 bis summaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have a number -- I'm not sure what the total number is that's prepared now that we could read in. I don't know if the Court wanted today in terms of housekeeping matters also to maybe address some things in connection with the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have drawn the attention of the parties to the specific list made by Ms. Philpott showing only those exhibits that had not yet been decided upon. And I think I asked the parties to prepare any submissions or objections in relation to those exhibits. We could start with it now. We could also have an early break and do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I request that we have an early break because it also involves Ms. Loukas and I suggested to Ms. Loukas that she should come along now and be available immediately after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be very practical. Would there be any other issue the parties would like to raise after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have one, Your Honour, I would like to bring to the Court's attention. Before the recess, the Court asked us to reduce our number of remaining 92 bis witnesses for the municipalities. I think we had 113, and we were asked to reduce it to 61. We provisionally have a list of 61. And in connection with that, since our project on agreed facts from the municipalities is not working any more, I think we have to revive our process for our submissions of the 92 bis materials, any Defence objections, and the Court decisions on which witnesses' evidence will be admitted that way, which ones will have to come from cross-examination, et cetera. And we would like to discuss the schedule in regard to that because we have some municipalities that we've already begun where we have some of those witnesses pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will adjourn now, and we'll then continue perhaps we take a bit more time for the break this time. After 40 minutes, that would be at 11.00 we'll resume, and we'll start with the reading in the transcripts of 92 bis summaries, and we'll then deal with the exhibits.

utterances.text: Before we start dealing with exhibits and reading into the transcript of 92 bis summaries, I first want to revisit a matter we dealt with just prior to the break, and that is the following: You asked, Mr. Hannis, whether the Chamber had any preference for finishing the next witness by Monday, and I said, no there's no specific reason why. utterances.text: As far as the schedule, Your Honour, there's no problem with sitting further on Monday. I believe the witness was scheduled for four hours of direct exam. utterances.text: Your Honour, absolutely no problem at all about Your Honour's suggestion about Monday. In fact, that would in principle be preferable to the Defence because it's always good to have a completely clear day to work away from the Court. utterances.text: I do understand. I fully appreciate that under 89(F) it's not exactly the same. utterances.text: Your Honour, we are going to begin by reading some summaries of 92 bis witnesses. utterances.text: So that's available to the translators. Perhaps I explain once more to the public why we do this exercise at all. There's not much public at this moment. But we do it because the procedure under Rule 92 bis under which written statements can be introduced into evidence makes it unclear for the outside world what approximately has been admitted into evidence, and therefore a short summary of what that evidence is about is read in court in order to serve the best of the ability of this Chamber the public character of the trial. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll begin with a Bratunac witness, Witness 129, Dzevad Gusic. Mr. Dzevad Gusic took over as president of the SDA in Bratunac on 20th March 1992. In this role, he met with leading members of the SDS including the president of the SDS municipal board, Mr. Miroslav Deronjic. Mr. Gusic describes the way in which nationalistic tensions increased during 1992 in Bratunac. He states that nationalist meetings of Serbs were held in cafes where Serbs would gather and sing Chetnik songs. Furthermore, posters and slogans appeared on walls insulting Muslims and promoting Serb nationalism. He recalls the comment of senior SDS official that the Serbs were willing to use 200.000 of their own people "so that 2 million Muslims would disappear." He describes beatings of prominent Muslims and the firing of automatic weapons during the night. From late 1991, Mr. Gusic received information that the JNA and the SDS were working together to arm the Serb civilians. By early 1992, Mr. Gusic observed that his local Serb neighbours held automatic weapons in their possession. And by this time, they were displaying their weapons with a great degree of arrogance. Mr. Gusic describes an incident when a unit of the JNA came from Ljubovija, Serbia and demanded that the head of the National Defence, Mr. Becirovic, hand over the files listing men eligible for mobilisation. A crowd of between 2.000 and 4.000 people resisted the JNA's efforts to obtain the files and eventually the JNA officers withdrew, having failed to obtain the files. He also refers to the ambush of a car containing four Muslims by Serb gunmen in the village of Kravica in September 1991 when two Muslim leaders were killed. Both the Serb leader Nikola Koljevic and high-level leader of the SDA, Ejup Ganic, attended Bratunac city and assured the local people that justice would be done. Following this joint assurance, Koljevic travelled to Kravica and assured the local population of Serbs that an investigation would not take place. In late 1991, Mr. Gusic observed that the JNA had installed artillery weapons and mortars in positions on the hills overlooking Bratunac with the barrels facing towards the town. At this time, Mr. Gusic received information that the JNA regulars were training local Serb civilians in the village of Vranesevic. A meeting took place with the JNA and the SDS where the issue of the JNA training local Serbs was discussed. The JNA representatives provided vague responses to this allegation, including the excuse that the unit conducting the training was not under local control and had been brought in from outside the area. Soon after the meeting with the JNA and SDS officials, a further meeting was held with Miroslav Deronjic and his assistants. He demanded that the police be divided because the Serb people felt that they were in a minority and were under direct threat from the Muslims. He threatened the Muslim representatives stating that if they did not comply "Muslims would disappear." Deronjic stated that he was under the direct control of Radovan Karadzic and that Karadzic was pressuring him to "get this division underway." Mr. Gusic spoke with SDS representatives on a daily basis during his time in political office. The SDS representatives gave assurances that everything was going to be fine. During these meetings, Deronjic spoke about having regular meetings with Radovan Karadzic and attempted to use this as a lever to ensure that the Muslims agreed to the SDS demands. He used as an example the village of Janja in Bijeljina where Muslims had accepted all Serb demands and no harm had subsequently come to them. Mr. Gusic was personally threatened between 20th of March 1992 when he took over the Presidency of the SDA and 17th April 1992 when Bratunac city was taken over. One evening, when Mr. Gusic left his house, automatic fire passed over the roof of this house and he returned the fire with one round from his pistol. A Serb, Tihomir Mrakic, told Mr. Gusic that if it was known who fired the shot from Mr. Gusic's yard then it would be "very bad for him." On another occasion when leaving his house, a young Serb man pulled out a pistol and fired shots over Mr. Gusic's head. On 17th April 1992, Mr. Gusic observed that a Serb military unit had arrived in the town and formed a guard around the Hotel Fontana. He went to the police station and spoke to the chief of police, Senad Hodzic. The president of the municipality, Nijaz Dubicic and professor of physics, Numo Pleho, joined this meeting. Miroslav Deronjic came to the police station and instructed the Muslim leaders to go to the Hotel Fontana ask meet with the leadership of the Serb military unit. At the Hotel Fontana, the Serb soldiers in JNA uniform stated that Bratunac was a Serb municipality and that they were taking control. Mr. Gusic and the other Muslim representatives were warned that if a single shot was fired by a Muslim, then the whole family of the person who fired the shot would be eliminated. The military leaders gave a deadline of two to three hours for the police to surrender and hand over their weapons. The Muslim leaders were told to produce a list of all Muslims in the area that were nationalists and that they were going to "settle accounts." Following this meeting, the Muslim delegation were to meet with Miroslav Deronjic at a nearby office. On the way, he observed a group of 40 to 50 uniformed local Serbs loading weapons. When he met with Deronjic, Deronjic stated that everything would be okay, but said that he had no choice in imposing this Serb authority and that it had to be this way. He said there could be no -- there could be joint government and that nothing bad would happen. Following the meeting with Deronjic, the Muslim delegation returned to the police station. At 3.00, soldiers, officers, and Miroslav Deronjic arrived at the police station and began to kick in the doors and searched for and seized the police weapons. Mr. Gusic tried to get away from the police station, and prior to being allowed to leave he was told that he must prepare a list of Muslim extremists and nationalists and that if he did not comply he would be killed. In order to escape, Mr. Gusic promised to provide the list the following day and on this understanding he was allowed to go. Mr. Gusic was aware of what had happened in other municipalities in Bosnia and decided that he had to leave the area as soon as possible. Mr. Gusic left the area and made his way through a number of Serb checkpoints towards Kladanj. Mr. Gusic travelled with the Bratunac police chief, Senad Hodzic. Mr. Hodzic was an acquaintance of the Vlasenica police chief, Mr. Bjelanovic, who was a Serb. Bjelanovic provided safe passage for the Muslim leaders through Vlasenica, and the Muslim leaders were able to complete their escape to safe Bosnian territory and seek refuge. Your Honours, the second summary is of Witness 131, Mr. Ahmo --
