utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly. The next witness is Witness 131, Mr. Ahmo Ibisevic from Bratunac. Mr. Ahmo Ibisevic was born in the village of Hranca in Bratunac Municipality. In 1978, he moved to Bratunac town where he lived until the beginning of the war. He states that prior to the elections in late 1990, the SDA and the SDS were allied in their goal to get rid of the communist party. However, with the formation of the national parties, the Muslim peoples started to gather around the SDA, and the Serbs around the SDS. Differences in ethnicity started to be the main ground of political life. After the elections, the appointments to offices in the local government and in local industry were divided on an equal basis between Muslims and Serbs. Mr. Ibisevic describes the incident in Bratunac when a JNA unit came to the centre of the town to seize lists of all military-aged men from the secretariat of National Defence. He states that the Muslims resisted the JNA's attempts to seize the documents. At the beginning of 1992, ethnic tensions in Bratunac increased. The ethnicities became increasingly divided. Mr. Ibisevic states that it was no longer possible to talk to Serb people because they would immediately respond stating that the Muslims had their Green Berets ready and that they were "fully armed" and other accusations of that nature. As a result, Bosniaks only went to Muslim pubs and restaurants and Serbs only went to Serb pubs and restaurants. In the Serb pubs, Chetnik songs were sung, and SDS or other Serb nationalist graffiti was spread all over the town. After the referendum for independent of Bosnia was held at the beginning of March 1992, the conditions of life in Bratunac degenerated very quickly. At this stage, Muslims who had been residing in the town for a long time decided to leave. The Serbs openly threatened Muslims in the street. They told the Muslims to leave the town, and although the Serbs were not carrying their weapons openly at this time, gunfire could be heard in Serb villages. By the beginning of April 1992, Mr. Ibisevic saw Serbs in the countryside and in Serb villages openly carrying automatic weapons. Mr. Ibisevic was informed by the villagers of Hranca village that JNA military trucks had been approaching Serb villagers during the preceding days. At this time, the JNA was composed almost entirely of Serbs because the Muslim soldiers had deserted their units after the events in Croatia. After the attacks by Serb forces on Bijeljina and Zvornik to the north of Bratunac along the Drina, the Serbs in town threatened the Muslims in Bratunac stating that Bratunac would be the next town to be attacked. At this time, many Muslims fled to Srebrenica, Tuzla, and Kladanj. At this time, the Muslims who remained were even afraid to walk along the streets. During this time, several tanks had been deployed in the Ljubovija area in Serbia with their cannons aimed towards the town of Bratunac. On 17th April 1992, a military convoy of paramilitaries came to Bratunac. Members of the Seseljevci and the Bijeli Orlovi and JNA units were present in the town. Soldiers in full combat gear arrived, and they patrolled the streets with armoured vehicles, tanks, and other military vehicles. They were armed with automatic rifles, portable machine-guns, heavy machine-guns, hand grenades, and every kind of weapons. On the vehicles, heavy-barrel machine-guns were mounted. In less than two hours, they established military control over the whole town. Muslims were told to stay inside their houses or they would be killed. Over a period of two days, the Muslim policemen were disarmed. Muslims in the municipal leadership were dismissed, and Muslims were fired from their jobs and told to leave Bratunac. The headquarters of the Serb military forces were set up in the MUP building, Hotel Fontana, and a part of the Vuk Karadzic School. Mr. Ibisevic could see the school facilities from the window of his apartment. He observed the Serb officer Dragan Josipovic at the Vuk Karadzic School. Mr. Ibisevic moved out of the town centre to the village of Hranca on 23rd of April 1992 where he stayed in his father's house. On around 27th April 1992, Mr. Ibisevic received a telephone call from a colleague of his who worked at the Vuk Karadzic School and she requested that he attend to the school to report for work obligations. He attended the school and observed that soldiers were guarding the entrance to the gymnasium of the school. He found out later that there were Muslim inmates already inside the gym. On the morning of 3rd May 1992, the village of Hranca was surrounded by armoured vehicles and members of the Serb TO and paramilitaries. The Serbian forces fired their infantry weapons at the villagers killing a 6-year-old daughter. They captured two men, tortured them, and killed them. Nine men were taken away and never seen again. They gathered the women and children and old men and tortured them, forcing them to lie on the ground and firing infantry weapons over their heads. They torched 43 houses in the Ramici hamlet and ordered the villagers from this hamlet to go to the Meljemi hamlet. The majority of Serb Territorial Defence members were neighbours of Mr. Ibisevic. He was able to identify by name 11 members of that unit. On 4th May 1992, there was gunfire from the direction of Radovici and the Hranca villagers were disturbed again. On 9th May 1992, Hranca was surrounded again by the Serb Territorial Defence members and paramilitaries and fired upon. In the hamlets of Cerovac and Polje, about 60 houses were torched. In this attack, Serb forces shot dead 11 local villagers. On 11th May 1992, Miladin Jokic and Dragan Ilic, Serb policemen Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond from Bratunac, came to the house of Alija Sulejmanovic and Bajro Sulejmanovic and told them that the villagers should all gather at Abdulah Ramic's house and that everyone would be taken to Kladanj and exchanged. About 250 villagers gathered and were taken by buses of the Vihor company to the municipal hall in Bratunac. A member of the Serbian TO ordered men to get off the bus. They lined up and forced to sing Chetnik songs and surrender their valuables. Milan Trsic, a driver in the Vihor company, was dressed in camouflage uniform and he struck the men with a whip. The men, who were about 60 in number, were then marched to the Vuk Karadzic school. The women and children were taken to Kladanj. At the Vuk Karadzic school, Mr. Ibisevic witnessed beatings and killings and saw a number of dead bodies lying on the ground covered in blood. Mr. Ibisevic saw the head of the MUP, Savo Babic at the Vuk Karadzic gymnasium on two occasions. When Babic entered, there were dead bodies lying on the floor. He was detained at the Vuk Karadzic school until 14th of May 1992 and then transferred to Pale and later exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we thought we'd alternate every couple witnesses just for the sake of the audience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to save your voice and keep us awake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, the next witness is a witness for whom a pseudonym was requested. I'll be referring to this witness KRAJ 128 from Bratunac. The witness was born in the village of Glogova in the Municipality of Bratunac and lived there until 9 May 1992 when the village was attacked by Bosnian Serb military forces. The witness was one of the founders of the SDA party in Bratunac and held positions of President of the SDA in Glogova and President of the Executive Board of the SDA in Glogova. When the SDA and the SDS were formed, they were formed with the common goal of overthrowing the old communist party, and the relationship between the parties was fairly good. After the elections, the Serbs gathered only around members of their own nationalist party, and the relationships between the parties and the different ethnicities deteriorated. Soon, Serbs only socialised with Serbs, and Muslims only with Muslims. Serb nationalistic graffiti was displayed all over the town, and Chetnik songs were played in Serb bars and cafes. The witness describes an incident in the town when a JNA unit entered the town and attempted to force the President of the National Secretariat of Defence, Dzemail Becirovic to hand over a list of military-aged personnel. He states that after this incident, relationships between Serbs and Muslims deteriorated further. The witness observes that all of the weapons which at one time were held by the Bratunac TO had been given over to the JNA. He also observes that after the Muslims refused to mobilise for the war in Croatia, the JNA was dominated by Serbs. Accordingly, he observes that it is easy to understand how weapons were distributed to Serb civilians. A further incident occurred in September 1991 where two Muslims were shot dead in the village of Kravica. After this incident, it was not safe to move around -- to move during the nighttime. Gunfire could be heard during the night. By January, February 1992, companies had stopped working, and prominent members of the Muslim community of Bratunac had left the municipality due to concerns as to their safety. In his role as a leader in the SDA, the witness learned that the leader of the SDS, Miroslav Deronjic, had close contacts with Radovan Karadzic. He states that after the referendum in early March 1992, the local SDS was instructed from Pale that they should proceed creating a Serb municipality in order to remain within the Yugoslav state. The Serb municipality of Bratunac was created immediately after the referendum. A Serb crisis staff was also created which was chaired by Miroslav Deronjic. Further, headquarters of the Serb police was set up in a new part of the municipality building close to the Vuk Karadzic School. The Serb police were created, and Serb checkpoints were set up on all the ways leading in and out of Bratunac town. On 17 April 1992, the witness was informed that Bratunac town had been taken over by fully armed Serb paramilitary units. On around 22 April 1992, a Muslim delegation from Glogova had a meeting with Miroslav Deronjic. Deronjic guaranteed the delegation that nothing would happen to the villagers of Glogova if they handed over all the weapons. At this time, the witness had already heard rumours that Serbs were organising the collection of all the weapons owned by Muslims. On 25 April 1992, nine APCs, other military trucks, and two police cars arrived in Glogova. Soldiers in JNA uniform and full combat gear were spread all over the road. They declared themselves as Novi Sad Corps coming from Serbia to gather all weapons owned by both Serb and Muslim villagers. The witness realised that this was not true because he recognised one of the members of the unit was a reservist and not a professional JNA soldier. He also recognised eight local Serb policemen in the group. The soldiers searched the houses in Glogova for weapons and gathered the male villagers in front of the school. When the witness returned to his house, he was grabbed by a soldier and threatened. He was then escorted to the school. The chief of the Serb police, Milutin Milosevic and one of the soldiers informed the men that all weapons had to be handed over in two days' time. The witness handed over his hunting rifle on that day and received a receipt from it from the JNA officer. The witness also observed that the soldiers had a list with the names of all persons who possessed weapons of any kind. On 27 April 1992, the same Serb soldiers and police returned to the village to collect the weapons. The villagers who remained handed over their registered weapons. They were told by Milutin Milosevic on behalf of Miroslav Deronjic that the safety of the village was guaranteed. During the following days, Serb policemen visited the village of Glogova and asked for automatic rifles to be handed over. On 3 May 1992, the village of Hranca was attacked and people fled to shelter in Glogova. On 9 May 1992, armoured vehicles approached Glogova and the village was attacked with heavy gunfire. The witness escaped to the woods from where he observed the takeover. The entire village was surrounded and Serb soldiers moved toward the centre of town discharging their automatic weapons. Houses in the external part of the village were set on fire. The witness sheltered with 11 other men from Glogova in a dugout on the side of the hill. Local Serb soldiers found the witness and the other men in their shelter and marched them to the centre of the town. The witness was ordered together with 22 other men and 3 male children to line up --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My apologies. The witness was ordered together with 22 other men and 3 male children to line up in front of the shopping centre. Three men, including the witness, were taken out of the group and loaded into a nearby car. While the witness was walking toward the car, the other men were ordered to move in the direction of the mosque. The commander of the group of soldiers directed a soldier with a machine-gun to go in the direction of the other prisoners. After a while, the witness heard gunfire and people screaming. He later heard that the men had been executed at the back of the mosque. When the gunfire finished, the commander drove away from the centre of the town, and the car the witness was in followed the commander's car. The witness was taken to the Serb SUP in Bratunac where the commander told a Serb police officer that the witness and the two other men had to be interrogated. The officer told the commander to take the witness and the others to the Vuk Karadzic School. The witness was taken to the gym of the school that was empty. He was guarded by two Serb police officers. After some time, six or seven Serb soldiers came into the gym and beat the witness and the other two men severely. The witness heard another person being beaten and was able to subsequently identify this man as a Muslim from Hranca. The men were interrogated and then beaten again over a period of seven hours. The soldiers were asking for information in relation to weapons. The witness told the soldiers that he had a pistol stored in the shelter where he had been hiding earlier in the day. He was taken to the shelter by two soldiers. One of the soldiers sat in the car whilst another entered the shelter looking for the weapon. At that moment, the witness made his escape. The witness states that 65 to 70 villagers were killed in the attack on Glogova, including men, women, and children. Houses were plundered, and 80 per cent of them were set on fire. I'll do one more, and then exchange with Mr. Gaynor. The next witness is KRAJ 126, Dzemail Becirovic from Bratunac. Prior to the war, Mr. Becirovic was Secretary for National Defence in the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac Municipality. He grew up in the Bratunac Municipality, and prior to 1992, he had lived in the municipality all of his life. He was 31 years old when he left the municipality. He states that prior to 1989, there were weapons stores in the municipality maintained by the Territorial Defence. However, these weapons were removed. Whilst it was said that they were being taken to the army barracks in Tuzla, these weapons were, in fact, taken in the direction of Serbia. The nearest JNA unit to the Bratunac Municipality was located in Ljubovija Municipality in Serbia. On a hill nearby Ljubovija, there was an army barracks. Sometime in 1991, a tank unit arrived at this barracks. The witness went to Ljubovija, and he saw this unit on the hill with their barrels pointing toward Bratunac. There were no JNA barracks in the Municipality of Bratunac. Mr. Becirovic was one of the early members of the SDA party in Bratunac. The SDS party was formed in Bratunac in October or November 1990. Mr. Becirovic attended the constitutional assembly of the SDS in Bratunac which was held in the stadium in Bratunac. At this assembly, Velibor Ostojic gave a speech during which he claimed that the Muslims had a plan to link Bosnia and Sandzak and Podrinje. He was given ovations and was cheered by the Serbs who were present. He said that the Serbs would never permit BiH to become an independent country and the Serbs would never permit themselves to be separated from their mother country, Serbia. After the elections in 1990, Mr. Becirovic was appointed to the position of secretary for national defence. In the course of his involvement in the municipal assembly and the executive board, Mr. Becirovic observed that it was very difficult for the government to accomplish anything in the municipality because there were constant disagreements between the Serb and Muslim representatives. By way of example, Mr. Becirovic describes a proposal made by the president of the executive board, Radoljub Djukanovic, a Serb, in relation to the emergency supplies that were held in a central store in Bratunac. Djukanovic proposed that all emergency supplies be divided between 11 villages, 9 of which were Serb villages. Despite the fact that this was not agreed to by the executive board, Djukanovic faxed this decision to Sarajevo. However, the decision was intercepted by a Bosniak working in the communications office, and the decision was not implemented. When the war started in Croatia, Mr. Becirovic was ordered by Major Gavric of the Tuzla Corps to mobilise a unit to distribute the call-up orders. Whilst he issued the mobilisation calls as he had been ordered to do, he also sent out a message to all the Bosniak persons not to respond to the mobilisation. In the end, only a few Serbs were sent to the battlefields in Croatia. There were two further mobilisation calls that the Muslims did not answer. In 1991, when the Serbs realised that they could not pass decisions in the executive board, they formed a crisis staff. They started to mobilise Serb fighters for the war in Croatia through the crisis staff. Mr. Becirovic learned at this time that the Serbs intended to take all the records held in the municipal office of men eligible for military service. On 27 August 1991, Mr. Becirovic removed those records and hid them. Miroslav Deronjic and five or six other members of the Serb Crisis Staff came to Mr. Becirovic's office and told him that he would be killed if he did not return the records within 24 hours. Deronjic was angry and shouted at Mr. Becirovic. He pointed at a map and said that the Muslims had nothing to look forward to in the area and that the area was all part of Greater Serbia. Mr. Becirovic went to Sarajevo where he was told by the Minister of Defence, Mr. Djoko, to retain the records. When he returned from Sarajevo, there was a group of 200 to 300 local Serbs in front of the National Defence building. Members of the group demanded the return of the records. The crowd built in the city centre. And at around 2.00 p.m. in the afternoon, a JNA unit from Ljubovija in Serbia arrived, and the Muslim leaders were told that the JNA would not withdraw without at least the documents for the Serbs. The JNA were resisted by Muslim police, and a few hours later the JNA withdrew without the records. By around September 1991, the Serbs had obtained armaments. The armaments were obtained from Serbia. They were transported in boats across the Drina River. In around September 1991, in the village of Kravica, a vehicle carrying four Muslims was ambushed by Serbs and two Muslim men were shot and killed. Nikola Koljevic came to Kravica and informed the Serbs that the legal authorities would not investigate the case. As a result of this shooting, and the failure to prosecute the perpetrators, the relationships between Serbs and Muslims worsened. In order to cool down the situation, the head of police and commander were dismissed by a committee consisting of Muslims and Serbs. During this period, an order came from Sarajevo to enlarge the reserve police force and arm them with weapons. This calmed down the Muslim part of the population since they were a majority -- there were a majority of Muslims in reserve police force. In early April 1992, Deronjic stated that they wanted to establish a Serbian police force. By this time, there was JNA artillery in the hills on the Serbian side, and there was a regular army unit that had arrived and settled in the village of Vranesevici. The Serbs promised they would withdraw if the Muslims agreed to the establishment of a Serbian police force. On 9 April 1992, the Serbian crisis staff stated that a Serb police force would be formed either with or without the Muslims' agreement. In order to keep the peace, on 10 April 1992, it was agreed at an assembly session that a Serbian police would be formed. From 10 April 1992 to 17 April 1992, there were parallel police forces. During this period, the Muslim population was being threatened and told to "move away." On 17 April 1992, a group of Arkanovci soldiers arrived at the Hotel Fontana and took it over. They invited the president of the municipality and the president of the SDA to a meeting and told them that the Muslims must surrender completely. Mr. Becirovic left Bratunac for Konjevic Polje. On the way, he passed through checkpoints manned by Serbian police. He heard that in the afternoon of 17 April 1992, Muslim police surrendered their weapons and the civilian authorities surrendered all legal power to the Serbian crisis staff. He did not personally observe what occurred in Bratunac, however, Mr. Becirovic heard there were many arrests and killings and expelling of inhabitants. Mr. Becirovic observed several convoys of people passing by escorted by Serb police. Mr. Becirovic heard that males had been taken to Pale. Mr. Becirovic saw smoke coming from the village of Glogova, and inhabitants from Glogova came through the woods to Konjevic Polje where they informed the people that their village had been completely burned down. They also said that a group of unarmed civilians had been gathered by the Serbs and killed. Mr. Becirovic organised the local people in the village for defence against the Serb forces. On one occasion, a regular JNA unit with APCs and trucks entered the village intending to seize the weapons without fighting. The local people resisted them and they withdrew. By 15 May 1992, the villagers had blocked the road around their village, stopping the movement of JNA army units between Sarajevo and Serbia. On 29 May 1992, there was a heavy attack on Konjevic Polje from Kravica by artillery. Around noon, a convoy of heavy vehicles started moving toward the defence line. They attacked, and about 30 grenades fell in around one minute. Infantry units were also moving toward the village. The Muslims captured an APC that tried to pass over their barricade. Using the APC and a rocket launcher, the villagers in Konjevic Polje managed to defend their village. They destroyed the first tank that was approaching with the rocket launcher and the attack was stopped. The Serb forces did not know this was the only rocket the Muslims had, otherwise they would have captured the village easily. Later, Mr. Becirovic heard that the Serbs had 44 casualties. Some of the fighters were not local people but were from Serbia. The attacks on Konjevic Polje continued through 1992 including bombs by MiG aircraft. However, by 1992 the Serbs had not succeeded in capturing the area. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next witness is Mujo Dracic, Witness 025 from Bosanski Petrovac. Prior to the war in Bosnia, Mr. Dracic worked as a shopkeeper in the village of Bjelaj in the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac. Before the 1990 elections, the witness did not notice any tensions between different ethnic groups. After the forming of the SDS party, however, things began to change. Mr. Dracic noticed that Serbs separated themselves from Muslims and began to sing nationalistic songs. Serbs also stopped coming into the witness's shop and would only go into Serb-owned shops. In the 1990 elections, the SDS party won, and in Bjelaj Milorad Vekic of the SDS party was elected president of the community. The local Serb police ordered Muslims to turn in any weapons they might have. Uniformed Serbs patrolled the village, and on several occasions came into the witness's shop, called him derogatory names, and threatened him. In June of 1992, after the outbreak of war, four officers wearing the old regular police uniforms came into Mr. Dracic's shop, arrested him, and took him to the Bosanski Petrovac police station. The police station was full of detained Muslim citizens. While he waited, the witness observed Serb police bringing more Muslims to the station. The Serb police were brutally beating the arrestees. The witness was interrogated by a Serb police officer wearing the regular police uniform. The officer put a pistol to the witness's head and asked him about a rifle. The witness did not own a rifle and told this to the officer. The officer questioned the witness ten times, each time holding the pistol to the witness's head. He also threatened to put the witness in the Manjaca, Kozila, or Kamenica prison camps. For three days, Mr. Dracic was held at the police station with 40 other men in a room measuring 3 metres by 3 metres. During this time, the detainees were denied access to a bathroom and were taken out for interrogations and beatings. After his release, Mr. Dracic went out into the street and saw army soldiers from Orasac shooting into the air and throwing hand grenades. The soldiers wore grey uniforms, long army coats, and the kokarda on their hats. The witness was able to make it to Bjelaj where he was stopped by Milorad Sovilj who wore a grey-olive JNA uniform and helmet and carried a machine-gun. Sovilj swore at Mr. Dracic and told him that he had killed his family and that he was leaving him alive so he could see all of his family dead. When the witness arrived at his home, he saw that his family was still alive. Mr. Dracic and his family and Muslim neighbours were terrorised night after night. Soldiers wearing olive-grey JNA uniforms shot out all of the windows in their homes and set fire to a nearby haystack. These nightly attacks culminated on 22 September 1992 when Serbs wearing JNA uniforms fired a shoulder-mounted anti-tank rocket known as Zolja into the witness's home. Mr. Dracic put his wife, children, and 80-year-old mother into the water well in the basement. He remained upstairs to watch the uniformed men who were outside swearing and shooting at his house. They set fire to his garage. The uniformed men then moved on to Mr. Dracic's neighbour's house. The witness heard ten explosions, and then saw his neighbour's house and barn erupt into flames. He heard the screams of the animals as they burned trapped inside the barn. Mr. Dracic hid in the basement well in the water with his wife, children, and mother until 8.00 the next morning. He subsequently learned that two of his neighbours had been burned alive in the fire. In late September 1992, the witness and his family then fled to the village of Busije. The nightly burning of houses by JNA-uniformed men continued. And from this point on, Mr. Dracic and his family and other Muslims slept outside at night out of fear of being burned alive. From 22nd September 1992 until 22nd of January 1993, the witness observed Serbs looting, shooting at, and burning Muslim houses every night. Muslims who were seen on the street were beaten or killed. In the midst of the war, Mr. Dracic met Milorad Vekic, the SDS party community president. Vekic told the witness: "Do you dare to walk around the village? In our headquarters, it says we are to destroy even Muslim cattle if we find them." On 22nd January 1993, the witness and his family were able to leave the area where they were exchanged under the auspices of the International Red Cross for Serbs in Bihac. The next witness is Midho Druzic, Witness 309 from Bosanski Petrovac. Mr. Druzic worked as a truck driver for a large timber factory in Bosanski Petrovac from 1974 until 1992. In 1990, he joined the SDA party and was elected as a member of the SDA executive board in Bosanski Petrovac. In November 1990, Mr. Druzic was elected as an SDA representative to the municipal assembly and remained an assemblyman until 1992. The witness was present at an SDS rally held in Bosanski Petrovac. The rally was attended by local SDS representatives and also by guests from Serbia. One of the key speakers at the rally was Bogdan Kecman from Kosovo. The witness was especially struck by his speech by included the statement: "If the Muslims do not want to stay with us in Yugoslavia, we will have them impaled." In April 1992, Mr. Druzic was summoned into his manager's office and fired along with all other Muslims who worked at the company. In May 1992, the police called for all Muslims to hand in their weapons. The witness complied and turned in a hunting rifle to the police. On the 24th of May 1992, eight local Serb police officers came to the witness's home. The officers tied the witness up and searched his house. The police took the witness to the SUP where he was interrogated and then placed in solitary confinement without food or water for 30 hours. On the 15th of June 1992 Mr. Druzic was again arrested and taken to the SUP. Twenty-nine other Muslim residents of the area were also in custody, some of whom the witness recognised. For two weeks, these 30 men were detained in the kitchen of the local Serb police station, a room measuring approximately 4 metres by 6 metres. No charges were filed against the witness, and no reasons given for his arrest. On the 1st of July 1992, at 3.00 a.m., the officer on duty ordered the men out of the SUP station and into a waiting bus. The bus delivered the men to the prison camp at Kozila. Kozila is listed in schedule C of the indictment as detention facility 6.1. Miso Zuric, a former guard at Luca prison in Bihac was head of the camp. He ordered the men to remove all their personal belongings and valuables. Mr. Druzic was held in the Kozila prison camp for seven weeks. The camp was heavily guarded with machine-gun nests that were visible to the prisoners. Mr. Druzic was held in a room with approximately 17 other men. The prisoners ate, slept, urinated and defecated in this same room. The guards and Miso Zuric, the head of the camp, regularly tortured Mr. Druzic and the other detainees. The tortured included severe beatings, threats of death, orders to perform highly degrading acts such as licking another prisoner's blood from a table and kissing a guard's bayonet, water submersion, and periods of solitary confinement. On the 6th of August 1992, Mr. Druzic and 15 other detainees were transferred to the prison camp at Kamenica. Kamenica is listed in schedule C to the indictment as detention facility 6.3. Approximately 60 men shared a room measuring 8 metres by 12 metres without facilities. The witness was held at Kamenica for three months. During that time, his weight dropped from 120 kilos to 58 kilos. He and the other prisoners were forced to do manual labour 12 hours a day. At times, detainees were called out for interrogations and beaten. During his time at Kamenica, the International Red Cross visited the camp twice. After the first visit, on August 28th 1992, conditions at the camp did not change. The occasional beatings continued, and the detainees were still subject to forced labour. On the 3rd of November 1992, after the second visit by the Red Cross, Mr. Druzic, along with all the other detainees at Kamenica was released and transferred to a collection centre in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next two witnesses are pseudonym witnesses from the Municipality 6 of Brcko. The first witness I will read is witness KRAJ 043. The witness was a Bosnian Muslim civilian living in Brcko in 1992. He was detained in Luka camp in Brcko on 11 May 1992. Upon his arrival, he and his fellow detainees were lined up against the wall of the hangar. The soldier who was in charge said, "Here, I brought you some more balijas." The Serbian soldiers present who called themselves Chetniks started beating the detainees and verbally abusing them. They said, "We'll kill you all. Nobody's going to save you." Goran Jelisic arrived five minutes later after one of the soldiers had called him from his office. He said he was the director of the collection centre and that the detainees had been brought there, that they would be interrogated, and who would be found guilty would be killed and who was going to be found not guilty would be released. Jelisic said he did not think there was a single balija who was not guilty. Goran Jelisic introduced himself to the group of additional detainees in front of the Hangar as Adolf, he said that he was in command of the group which blew up the bridge over the Sava River, and on this bridge about 100 people were killed during that explosion: Men, women, children, even small babies. He said that he had killed about 150 people in the Luka camp, and it wasn't all, he was going to continue. When he introduced himself, Goran Jelisic wore the uniform of the policemen of the former Yugoslavia. During the witness's first night in detention, he and his fellow detainees were pushed to the front of the hangar and were ordered to sit on a concrete floor. At about 7.30 or 8.00 p.m., the detainees heard singing of Chetnik songs, saying, "Balija, you've had it. There's a little left for you. We will exterminate you." During that night, the detainees' valuables such as watches and rings and their personal documents were taken from them. Before midnight, the door was opened and four volunteers were called for. Four men came outside and blows could be heard indicating that the volunteers were being beaten outside. They were moaning and begging, "Don't do that, we're not guilty of anything." The voice could be heard saying, "Lie down, lean your head against the grate." This was followed by a voice saying, "Don't, don't do that to me. Why me? I haven't done anything. I'm not guilty." This was followed by a silenced shot. Two or three minutes later, another shot was heard. On one occasion during his detention at Luka the witness was called out in a group of four detainees. The witness watched as two other men in his group were forced to kneel over a metal grate in the roadway and executed one after the other. After executing the second detainee, Goran Jelisic said, "Another balija less!" The witness had to load the bodies of the executed detainees on the back of a refrigerated truck parked at Luka. Groups of four detainees were taken out of the hangar between 25 and 30 times. After each of these groups left the hangar, only one or two of the group would return. On or about 16 May 1992, Major Jerkovic who was wearing a JNA uniform came into the hangar with Jelisic and informed the detainees that there would be no more killings or mistreatment. In early July 1992, the witness together with the other detainees from Luka were transferred to Batkovic detention camp in Bijeljina. The next witness, Your Honour, is KRAJ 214, also from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, just looking at the clock, how many more would be to be read?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two more, Your Honour, and they are both shorter than the others. This one is less than a page and the other one is about a page. KRAJ 214 was a Bosnian Muslim and a practicing iman. Soldiers including Goran Jelisic came to the witness's home the evening of the 15th of May 1992. He was there with his wife, two daughters, and four female refugees who were staying with the family. Jelisic demanded identification and money from the witness as well as his car keys. Jelisic confiscated some 15.600 marks from the witness, both personal savings and funds he held on behalf of the community. The soldiers drove the witness to the detention camp in his own car. At Luka camp, Goran Jelisic interrogated the witness in an office. During the interrogation, Jelisic sorted through a list of names held in a binder. Jelisic then handed this list to one of the soldiers in the room and ordered him to bring in the individuals whose names he had just circled. When the three Muslim men were brought in, Jelisic read out their names and asked them to identify themselves. After questioning, hitting, and humiliating these men, Jelisic ordered them to be taken outside. Jelisic then took a pistol from his desk and went outside. A few minutes later, the witness heard three muffled gunshots. After each gunshot, the witness heard screaming for help which stopped after the third gunshot. The witness believes these three men were killed. When Jelisic returned to the office, he asked the witness to "say a prayer for the men." Jelisic then resumed his interrogation of the witness. His interrogation included questions about two men, one who was the mayor of Brcko, and another who was the president of the SDA in Brcko. He accused Croats and Muslims of hating Serbs. He took his pistol and commenced a game of Russian roulette with the witness. He held the revolver to the witness's chest and fired but the gun did not discharge. He said, "Not even God wants you," and struck the witness. Jelisic then ended the interrogation. He gave the witness a yellow pass guaranteeing unfettered freedom of movement. On it was written: "The war presidency of the Municipality of Brcko." Jelisic signed this pass, "Adolf."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the final witness is Witness 045 , Hamdija Krupic from Bosanski Novi. Mr. Krupic was a policeman working in Bosanski Novi Municipality since 1975. He notes that the SDS won a majority of the vote in the 1990 elections. The president of the municipality was Radomir Pasic of the SDS. When the war in Croatia began, local Muslims refused to be mobilised to fight in Croatia. Serbs responded fully to the mobilisation. Checkpoints manned by members of the reserve military and regular police were set up at the entrances and exits to the town of Bosanski Novi. The police force reserve was also mobilised. Around the beginning of 1992, the tower at Mrakovica was physically turned so that only Serb TV could be received in the area. Mr. Krupic states that a paramilitary group called "Suha Rebra," which means "dry ribs" was formed. Its leader was Miroslav Petic. The witness says this group engaged in many "atrocities, raping, and looting" during the war. They performed work -- they performed work for the crisis staff. At the end of 1992 or the beginning of 1993, Muslim-owned businesses and homes started to be targeted with explosives. Krupic states that the official authorities in town were publicly against these bombings, but "in actuality, the SDS crisis staff was organising them." There was a breakdown in the chain of command within the police with conflicting orders being received from the republic level in Sarajevo and the regional level in Banja Luka. A special police unit from Banja Luka came to the municipality saying their task was to disarm extremists of all nationalities. Krupic says this group was under the command of Banja Luka CSB head Stojan Zupljanin. They wore red berets and were well armed. It transpired this special unit disarmed only Bosniaks. At the same time the SDS in Bosanski Novi was openly distributing weapons to the Serbs in villages and in the town. On 15th April 1992, all the police in Bosanski Novi were asked to sign an oath of loyalty to Serb authorities. The witness declined, saying he wouldn't wear the tri-colour Serb flag. The Serb police began wearing new blue camouflage uniforms like those worn by the special police in Belgrade. On 8th May 1992, the witness was told to turn in his police ID and weapons. He left town with his family the next morning. Upon returning to Bosanski Novi after the war, he noticed that in the villages of Blagaj and Suhaca, there are no mosques still standing and that many graveyards and tombs have been destroyed and damaged. The former mosque in Bosanski Novi has replaced by a border post. Your Honour, that ends the reading of the summaries of those particular witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. May I first make a small observation in relation to the summaries you've just read: These summaries are of such a detail it even goes beyond perhaps what it serves. Just to give you a few examples, if you are summarising the Witness Drazic and how his house was attacked you come up with a lot of details as dates and whether first the barn or the house, et cetera, where it would have done if you had stated, for example, that the witness states how his house and that of his neighbours were attacked, two of the latter burned alive when fire was set to the premises. That would, I would say, well have reflected. So dates, size of rooms, whether it was 4 by 6 metres or anything else, the Chamber thinks that a summary of approximately -- it's not the same for all the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond summaries, of course, but some of them could have been done in 40 per cent of what you actually used. Also, the emphasis should, I would say, be on the events rather than on the background and the history of how it came to attacks on villages. So therefore, the Chamber appreciates that a lot of work is given to summarise as precisely as possible, but it could be done a bit more efficiently. The list of exhibits which would be the next matter is rather long. So perhaps we not start it now and start at a quarter to 1.00 and adjourn until then.

utterances.text: We have now come to P217 and P218, two photographs; then the next one is P219 is a CD videoclip relating to Manjaca camp; and then we come to P219.A where there's still a problem. utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just make one further about P219, there was some confusion in this particular exhibit because there were B/C/S subtitles on the screen, there was English and B/C/S commentary, and the transcripts -- it was not entirely clear what the transcripts were reflecting. Part of the confusion arose because the subtitles inserted by the domestic television station were not precise translations of what was being spoken. So we have prepared a revised English transcript of what was said by the Sky News representative, by Paddy Ashdown and by the CNN representative, and a direct B/C/S translation of that. This is something which I've sent to the Defence. And we would suggest that these be substituted to the existing Exhibit P219.A and P219.A.1. And secondly, I would just like to make three brief submissions as to why these should be admitted into evidence. Three reasons are as follows: First of all, these constitute contemporaneous records of what was going on in Manjaca at the time, and their very contemporaneousness gives them added weight. Second, the Defence indicated on the record that the accused "did not know what was happening in Manjaca camp." Now, we submit that the transcripts of the CNN and Sky News reports demonstrate what was being said in the international news media at the time about Manjaca camp, and therefore these transcripts are relevant to the question of whether the accused knew or did not know about what was going on in Manjaca. The third reason we submit why these transcripts should be admitted is that the CNN representative Christiane Amanpour states "Karadzic himself authorised our visit to this camp" and given the proximity or alleged proximity between the accused and Karadzic, we submit that that is relevant evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first ask the Defence whether they have taken already a position in view of the new documents containing both undertitles and words spoken and translations to both of that.
